title: Heatwave Safety
description: Heatwaves are prolonged periods of excessively hot weather that can cause serious health problems. Knowing how to prevent, recognize, and respond to heat-related illnesses can save lives.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A heatwave is a prolonged period of excessively hot weather, which may be accompanied by high humidity. Heatwaves can cause heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and other serious health problems, particularly in vulnerable populations such as the elderly, children, and those with chronic illnesses. India experiences severe heatwaves during summer months, with temperatures often exceeding 45°C in many regions. Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves globally. Understanding heatwave safety is essential for preventing heat-related illnesses and deaths.

sections.heading: Before a Heatwave
sections.content: Monitor weather forecasts and heatwave warnings. Ensure your home is well-ventilated and consider using fans or air conditioning if available. Install window shades or blinds to reduce heat entering your home. Stock up on water and electrolyte drinks. Check on elderly neighbors, family members, and those with chronic illnesses. Plan outdoor activities for cooler times of day. Wear lightweight, loose-fitting, light-colored clothing. Know the signs of heat-related illnesses and have a plan for medical emergencies. Keep pets indoors with plenty of water.

sections.heading: During a Heatwave
sections.content: Stay indoors during the hottest part of the day, typically between 11 AM and 4 PM. If you must go outside, wear a hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen. Drink plenty of water even if you do not feel thirsty. Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and sugary drinks as they can cause dehydration. Eat light, cool meals. Take cool showers or baths to lower body temperature. Use fans to circulate air but remember fans do not prevent heat-related illness when temperatures are very high. Never leave children or pets in parked vehicles, even for short periods. Check on vulnerable people regularly.

sections.heading: Heat-Related Illnesses
sections.content: Heat exhaustion symptoms include heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, and muscle cramps. Move to a cool place, drink water, and cool the body with wet cloths. Heat stroke is a medical emergency with symptoms including high body temperature (above 40°C), hot and dry skin, confusion, seizures, and loss of consciousness. Call emergency services immediately for heat stroke. Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms caused by loss of salts and fluids—rest in a cool place and drink electrolyte solutions. Heat rash appears as red clusters of small blisters—keep the area dry and cool.

sections.heading: Vulnerable Groups
sections.content: Elderly people are at higher risk due to reduced ability to regulate body temperature. Infants and young children are vulnerable because their bodies heat up faster than adults. People with chronic illnesses such as heart disease, diabetes, and respiratory conditions are at increased risk. Those taking certain medications may have reduced heat tolerance. Outdoor workers are exposed to direct sunlight and physical exertion. Pregnant women and people who are overweight also face higher risks. Extra precautions should be taken to protect these vulnerable groups during heatwaves.

sections.heading: Safety Precautions
sections.content: Never leave anyone in a parked vehicle during a heatwave. Avoid strenuous physical activity during the hottest hours. Wear appropriate clothing that covers skin but allows air circulation. Use sunscreen to prevent sunburn, which affects the body's ability to cool down. Stay in air-conditioned buildings as much as possible during extreme heat. If you do not have air conditioning, visit public cooling centers or shopping malls during the hottest parts of the day. Keep your home cool by closing curtains on windows receiving direct sunlight. Follow official health advisories during heatwave alerts.
